name: Lama

catalog_citation: Ourso, Meterwa A. 1989. Phonological processes in the noun class system of Lama. Studies in African Linguistics 20(2): 151-178. DOI 10.32473/sal.v20i2.107452 (open access, journals.flvc.org/sal/article/download/107452/102772)
catalog_locator: p. 154, section 2.1 'Main features in Lama phonology', run-in subsection 'The tonal system'; restated in the section summary on p. 155.
catalog_quote: The tonal system. Lama has two basic tones, a high tone and a low tone. These tones combine to give two contour tones, a falling tone and a rising tone. The latter is never realized phonetically. It always surfaces as a low tone. [...] The falling tone is only realized phonetically on the final syllable of a word (said in isolation). In phrase medial position, the falling tone simplifies to a level high tone; the delinked low part can cause a following high tone to be downstepped in specific environments [Kenstowicz et al. 1988]. Lama starts then with two basic tones which in turn combine to give two additional tones. The overall tone configurations are High, Low, High-Low, and Low-High in the underlying representation. At the surface level only the first three configurations are allowed. The syllable, to which we now turn, is the tone bearing unit. [...] Lama has a two tone register, a high tone and a low tone. These tones combine into contour tones (a falling tone and a rising tone). The rising tone never surfaces whereas the falling tone only surfaces at phrase final position. Contour simplification is followed by tone spread one syllable to the right and downdrift. The syllable is the tone bearing unit.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

The rising tone never surfaces whereas the falling tone only surfaces at phrase final position. Contour simplification is followed by tone spread one syllable to the right and downdrift. The s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lama is a two-tone register language (H, L; contour HL surfaces only word/phrase-finally, LH never surfaces); the syllable is the tone-bearing unit, with high-tone spread one syllable rightward and downdrift. The source, like every other Lama description opened (Kenstowicz, Nikiema & Ourso 1988; Ourso & Ulrich 1990; Ulrich 1994), gives no rule for word stress and does not mention stress or accent at all; no positive claim of stress placement can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tonal notes: rising tone never surfaces, falling tone only at (phrase-)final position, downstep of a following H after a delinked L.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements are about tone on words said in isolation vs phrase-medial position (Kanté dialect). No stress domain is discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Ourso's descriptions (SAL 1989 article and the 1989 dissertation) describe the Kanté (Kandé) dialect of Lama, spoken in Kéran district; Aritiba 1983/1987 and Adjinare 2006 describe the Défalé/Refal (Doufelgou) and Kpaha varieties (Ulrich 1994: 'two attested dialects: Refal (Aritiba 1987) and Kanté (Ourso 1989a)'). All are under the single Glottolog language lama1275; no dialect glottocodes are assigned.

new_statements.quote: There are four tones in Lama; a high tone, a low tone, a falling tone, and a rising tone. At the surface level the rising tone is always realized as a low tone. To differentiate between the two types of low tone at the surface level, we will not mark the level low tone in our transcription. However, the low tone which is underlying a rising tone will be marked by a grave accent on the tone bearing unit (TBU). [pp. 153-154] ... The tonal system of the language has not been analyzed nor mentioned in Prost's analysis. [p. 9] ... The preceding chapter showed the syllabification processes in Lama. The conclusion of that chapter was that after meeting the segmental conditions, the syllable must also carry a tone to be well formed. [p. 140]

At the surface level the rising tone is always realized as a low tone.. will be marked by a grave accent on the tone bearing unit (TBU).' p. 9 (PDF 23) reads verbatim 'The tonal system of the language has not been analyzed nor mentioned in Frost's analysis' (scanned 'Frost' = Prost; the compiler normalized it). p. 140 (PDF 154) ch. 4 intro quote verbatim. p. 6 (PDF 20): 'This dissertation focuses on the Kante variant of Lama' verbatim; abstract (p. iii) says Lama is a Gur language of the districts of Keran and…
new_statements.relation_note: Same author as the existing SAL 20(2) statement; the dissertation refines it (four tones stated explicitly rather than 'two basic tones + two contour tones'; syllable = TBU; Prost 1963 had no tone analysis) and agrees that there is no word-stress statement. Access note: the IDEALS item page says download is restricted to the UIUC community, but the repository's own bulk endpoint (items/20531/bitstreams -> /downloads/<id>/file) served the PDF as item-20531.zip without login; recorded honestly; Describes the Kante variant only: 'This dissertation focuses on the Kante variant of Lama' (p. 6).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lama is described as a tone language with four tones (H, L, HL, LH; the rising tone always surfaces as low), with the syllable as tone-bearing unit and every well-formed syllable carrying a tone. The dissertation contains no section on stress or accent and never says where word stress falls or whether stress exists: the only hits for 'stress'/'accent' in 326 pages are a gloss 'na you (stressed form)' (p. 35, a pronoun form, not phonological stress) and the orthographic 'grave accent' used to mark the underlying rising tone.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress statement); tone chapters treat tonal exceptions in noun-class suffixation (§4.2.5) only
new_statements.identity_note: Ourso 1989 (dissertation) describes the Kante variant of Lama (district of Keran) explicitly, p. 6: 'This dissertation focuses on the Kante variant of Lama.' Aritiba 1987 (not opened) describes the Refal variant of Défalé (district of Doufelgou); Ourso p. 5-6 says the two variants are mutually intelligible dialects of one language. Brinneman & Ulrich 1995 is an SIL Lomé grammar of 'lamba', the administrative name for the same language [las].
